title: Thorium Valley | April 20, 2026
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley. A robot just ran a half marathon seven minutes faster than any human ever has. Fully autonomous — no remote control, no operator. Last year's winning robot time was 2 hours and 40 minutes. This year, under 51. A two-thirds improvement in twelve months. Not exactly incremental.

Gen Z is using AI just as much as last year but liking it a whole lot less. Excitement dropped 14 points. Anger jumped 9. Even daily users are souring. Apparently using something every day and actually wanting to are different things.

And Duke researchers found every major AI model aces creativity tests on its own — but they all ace them the exact same way. If everyone's using AI to stand out, nobody is.
toc: A robot just outran every human alive
Gen Z won't quit AI, but the enthusiasm is gone
AI is making everyone's work look the same

title: Thorium Valley | April 17, 2026
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley. The Pentagon tried to blacklist Anthropic for refusing to sign off on mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. Anthropic didn't budge. Two months later their revenue reportedly passed OpenAI's. Not exactly the outcome Hegseth was going for.

Workers swear AI saves them hours every week. A Danish study tied to government payroll records says the economic impact is zero. Stanford researchers have a word for what's filling the gap: workslop.

And OpenAI quietly turned Codex into something way bigger than a coding tool — nearly half its 3 million weekly users don't write code. Their head of Codex called it "the sneaky thing where we're building the super app in the open." At least they're owning it.

title: A leaked model name crashed an entire sector
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley. OpenAI bought a talk show. After a year of dead products, sycophancy backlash, and Forbes cataloging a graveyard of unfinished deals, I guess they figured if you can't win the narrative, buy the narrator.

Oracle laid off 30,000 people and told the SEC that AI code generation made them replaceable. Most companies at least dress that up as "restructuring." Stock's already down 25% this year, so the bar for a better strategy wasn't exactly high.

And a Texas CEO who fired 80% of his staff for refusing to use AI says he'd do it again without thinking twice. So much for the careful rollout everyone keeps promising. No shortage of conviction in today's stories. The receipts? Harder to come by.

title: Thorium Valley | March 20, 2026
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley.

An AI agent at Meta leaked restricted employee data last week — not from a hack, but because the agent didn't know it shouldn't. Existing security tools couldn't distinguish normal behavior from a breach until the damage was done, and that's a problem every company deploying agents is about to face.

Microsoft is retreating on a different front: over 11,000 people starred a GitHub project to rip AI out of Windows, and the company is now pulling Copilot from consumer apps while quietly redirecting everything toward enterprise, where the money is.

Washington wants to write one AI rulebook for all of it, which might be the most consequential story here if anyone can agree on what goes in it.

title: Thorium Valley | March 10, 2026
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley.

A survey of nearly 6,000 executives found over 80% of firms report zero productivity gains from AI—even as 70% actively use it and half a trillion dollars flows into infrastructure this year. Goldman coined a term for the disconnect: "AI-nxiety."

Nvidia is stepping back too, with Jensen Huang saying the company is done funding AI labs. He framed it as IPO timing, though the less comfortable read involves a chipmaker bankrolling its own biggest customers.

Then two OpenAI engineers built an internal data agent with the same tools the company sells externally—and it quietly became the most-used product in the building. Somewhere between the trillion-dollar uncertainty and the 82-second query, there's probably a realistic picture of where AI actually stands.

title: Thorium Valley | February 24, 2026
intro:
Good Morning Thorium Valley.

Artificial Analysis just overhauled its Intelligence Index — the scorecard many use to rank AI models — and the results are humbling. They replaced older academic-style benchmarks with real-world evaluations, and suddenly top models are scoring 50 or below on a 100-point scale.

Some of these same models were posting scores in the high 80s on the old tests. Turns out they'd gotten really good at passing exams without necessarily being useful. The AI equivalent of acing the SAT but struggling to file your taxes.

A federal judge accused the Pentagon of trying to "cripple" Anthropic for refusing to strip safety guardrails from Claude — the sharpest language yet in a case that could reshape how the government wields power over AI companies.
